The Bay whiff Citharichthys spilopterus is a small, left-eyed flatfish common in estuarine and coastal waters from the western Atlantic. Females of this species attain a considerably larger ultimate total length compared to males, with the maximum recorded size for females reaching 21 centimeters [Li = 21 centimeters]. This ultimate length serves as a reference for understanding the species' growth trajectory. In terms of reproductive development, females reach puberty at a total length of 11.7 centimeters [Lp = 11.7 centimeters], a size at which the onset of gonadal maturation becomes apparent. The mass of newly hatched yolk-sac larvae is remarkably low, reflecting the small size of the pelagic eggs from which they emerge. Specifically, the wet weight at birth has been documented at 0.22 milligrams [Wwb = 0.22 milligrams], a value consistent with the small egg diameter characteristic of this paralichthyid flatfish.

Egg diameter in this species typically ranges from 0.7 to 0.8 millimeters, and the resulting hatchling mass of 0.22 milligrams [Wwb = 0.22 milligrams] is a direct consequence of the limited yolk reserves contained within such small fertilised ova. Following eclosion, the yolk-sac larva undergoes a period of endogenous nutrition before transitioning to exogenous feeding. The adult wet weight corresponding to the ultimate total length provides an important benchmark for evaluating somatic growth. Females at their asymptotic length achieve a corresponding ultimate wet weight of 84.2 grams [Wwi = 84.2 grams], representing the maximum body mass typically attained in the population. At the point of sexual maturation, when individuals reach a length of 11.7 centimeters, the corresponding wet weight at puberty is 13.6 grams [Wwp = 13.6 grams]. This weight reflects the energetic investment required to reach reproductive competence in this demersal species.

Reproductive output in Citharichthys spilopterus has been quantified under controlled thermal conditions to establish potential fecundity limits. At a water temperature of 25.7 °C [T = 25.7 °C], gravid females display a maximum daily reproduction rate that can be expressed in terms of daily egg production. Under these warm conditions, field observations indicate that a single female can produce approximately 164 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 164 eggs per spawning event], with a spawning frequency of approximately one event per day, corresponding to about 164 eggs per day [Ri = about 164 eggs per day]. This high daily output is made possible by the batch-spawning strategy common among flatfishes, where multiple clutches are released over an extended spawning season. The elevated temperature of 25.7 °C likely accelerates ovarian recrudescence and vitellogenesis, thereby sustaining the maximum reproductive rate observed during the warmest months of the year in subtropical estuaries.

Longevity in the Bay whiff is influenced by ambient water temperature, as is typical for many teleost fishes. In cooler environments, metabolic rates are reduced and lifespan is extended. The maximum recorded lifespan for this species under cooler conditions, specifically at a mean annual temperature of 10.3 °C [T = 10.3 °C], is approximately 9 years [am = approximately 9 years]. This longevity estimate comes from field studies in the northern portion of the species' range, where seasonal temperatures are lower. At such temperatures, the fish experience slower growth rates and delayed reproductive schedules. The lifespan of 9 years [am = 9 years] observed at 10.3 °C [T = 10.3 °C] contrasts sharply with the accelerated life history observed in warmer waters, where individuals mature earlier but may have shorter lifespans due to heightened metabolic demands and increased predation pressure.

The transition from a pelagic larval stage to a benthic juvenile is a critical phase in the life cycle of the Bay whiff. After hatching, the yolksac larva remains in the water column for several days, relying on endogenous reserves from the egg. Once the yolk is fully absorbed, the exogenously feeding larva begins to capture small planktonic prey. Larval metamorphosis involves the migration of one eye to the opposite side of the head, a dramatic morphological transformation that prepares the fish for benthic life. Post-metamorphic juveniles then settle onto soft bottoms, where they adopt a cryptic lifestyle. Adults are iteroparous and broadcast spawners, releasing pelagic eggs that drift with currents. The species is an important component of estuarine food webs, serving both as predator of small invertebrates and as prey for larger piscivorous fishes and birds.
